title: Palate: structure
subtitle: Measuring what you feel
objectives: Judge sweetness, acidity, tannin, alcohol and body
Describe tannin by level and nature

steps.title: The five measures
steps.body: On the palate, judge sweetness from dry to luscious; acidity from low to high; tannin from low to high; alcohol from low to high; body from light to full. For still wines, alcohol is low below 11%, medium from 11 to 13.9%, high from 14%. Each measure stands on its own, so judge them separately.

steps.title: The nature of tannin
steps.body: Tannin has a level and a nature. Ripe tannins feel soft, fine-grained and velvety. Unripe tannins feel green, coarse and astringent. Oak tannins can feel dry and grainy. Tannin also interacts: high acidity makes tannin feel harsher; sugar and alcohol make it feel softer.
steps.highlight: Ripe tannin is soft; unripe tannin is coarse

steps.prompt: Which element tends to make tannin feel harsher?
steps.explanation: Acidity sharpens the perception of tannin. Sugar and alcohol soften it.

steps.title: Interactions
steps.body: Sweetness can mask acidity, so a sweet Riesling may seem less acidic than it is. Alcohol adds body and can taste sweet. Carbon dioxide adds freshness. Judge each element on its own scale, then consider balance: do they support each other, or does one stick out?
steps.highlight: Elements mask and support each other

steps.prompt: For still wines, alcohol of 14% or more is described as ____.
steps.explanation: 14% and above is high; 11 to 13.9% medium; below 11% low.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Judge sweetness, acidity, tannin, alcohol and body separately
Tannin has a level and a nature, ripe or green
Elements interact: sugar masks acid, acid sharpens tannin
